planting.note: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Diamante citron is among the most cold-sensitive of all citrus and requires a frost-free microclimate or container culture in most of zone 9.

directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in the warmest available microclimate. Diamante is the classic Italian citron cultivar, named for the coastal Calabrian town where it has been cultivated for centuries, grown almost entirely for its extraordinarily thick, sweet, aromatic white rind, which is the traditional source of candied citron peel used in panettone, fruitcake, and other European confections. The fruit itself is large, bumpy, and pale yellow, with relatively little pulp or juice compared to the mass of rind, and the whole fruit is typically processed rather than eaten fresh. Like other citrons it is quite cold-sensitive and benefits from a sheltered, frost-free site or container culture that can be moved to protection during freezes.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Rainforest Pearl Finger Lime (Pale Pink-White Caviar Lime Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; Rainforest Pearl is a finger lime cultivar selected for pale pink-white caviar-like pulp vesicles, a color prized by chefs for garnishing.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Rainforest Pearl bears slender, dark green fruit filled with pale pink to white, translucent, caviar-like pulp vesicles that burst with tangy citrus flavor, a color combination especially prized by chefs for garnishing seafood and desserts. It is self-fertile and, like other finger lime cultivars, bears at a younger age on grafted rootstock than most seedling-grown plants. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the pulp fresh as a garnish, since it does not store well once the fruit is opened.
sources: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries

common_name: Pink Ice Finger Lime (Pink-Blushed Caviar Lime Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; Pink Ice is a finger lime cultivar with a distinctive pink-blushed rind and pink pulp vesicles.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Pink Ice bears fruit with a distinctive rosy blush on the rind and pink, caviar-like pulp vesicles inside, adding visual appeal beyond the tangy citrus flavor common to all finger limes. It is self-fertile and bears at a younger age than seedling-grown plants when purchased grafted. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the pulp fresh as a garnish for seafood, cocktails, and desserts, since it does not store well once the fruit is opened.
sources: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries

common_name: Red Champagne Finger Lime (Reddish-Pink Caviar Lime Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; Red Champagne is a finger lime cultivar with reddish skin and pink-to-red caviar-like pulp vesicles.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Red Champagne bears fruit with a reddish-tinted skin and vivid pink-to-red, caviar-like pulp vesicles that burst with tangy citrus flavor, one of the more colorful finger lime selections available and popular with chefs for garnishing. It is self-fertile and bears at a younger age than seedling-grown plants when purchased grafted. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the pulp fresh, since it does not store well once the fruit is opened.
